Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:28: I heard from the mouth of my teacher, peace be upon him, a fine matter regarding vows as well. He said that when one vows to perform a commandment, at his utterance one angel is created, but its formation is not complete until the fulfillment of the commandment is completed — for it is known (see Avot 4:11) that whoever performs one commandment acquires for himself one defender; and if he vows and does not fulfill his vow, that angel is found suspended, and it is a suffering for it until that commandment's deed is completed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:29: Whoever wishes his prayer to be heard and his request granted should strive to fulfill his vows, as it is written, "offer to God thanksgiving, and pay your vows unto the Most High, and call upon Me in the day of trouble, I will deliver you, and you shall glorify Me" (Psalms 50:14-15), and so it is written in the book of Job, "you shall pray to Him, and He shall hear you, and you shall pay your vows; you shall also decree a thing, and it shall be established for you" (Job 22:27-28). These vows certainly refer to vows to Heaven, which it is a mitzvah to fulfill — this being what it says, "pay your vows unto the Most High" — for regarding permissible worldly matters, which are below, the phrase "your vows unto the Most High" would not fit properly. Now here is measure for measure: since in prayer he asks in speech that the Holy One, blessed be He, do such-and-such for him, He says to him, "You fulfill in deed what you have vowed, and I too will do and fulfill the request of your mouth that depends on speech" — and already known is what they say in the Zohar several times (Parashat Lech Lecha 77b), "arousal from below, arousal from above" — for one must always initiate the arousal from below first.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:30: Regarding the matter of vows as a "fence for separation," it is fitting for an intelligent person not to vow things that require formal annulment, but rather to vow for one day or half a day — as we find (Makkot 24a) Rabbi Yochanan, who used to say, "I am fasting until I get home" — this being [the concept of] "he swears to his own hurt and does not change" (Psalms 15:4). Even for a fast of hours, so that he can still recite "Answer us" [the prayer added on fast days], it is like this: he accepts upon himself, while it is still day, a fast until such-and-such an hour of the day, and afterward decides to complete the whole day in a fast, reciting "Answer us." This is a good device for one who is weak — that he accept a fast upon himself and not need to have his vow annulled the next day; and when he completes that day in holiness, he should accept upon himself another day like the previous one, so that all his days are found in repentance. But he should not accept to do such-and-such a number of consecutive fasts, for then his inclination will immediately stand against him with all its power to nullify him from his service; and if a person does his matters discreetly and outwits his inclination as Jacob did with Esau, he can take his blessing from his hand. Concerning something like this, it is possible that the psalmist intended in saying, "so will I sing praise to Your name forever, that I may daily perform my vows" (Psalms 61:9) — [performing them] day by day.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:31: However, so as not to forget to accept his vow for the next day, it is good that he find himself a companion to spur him on, or make a notebook and write his acceptance there, keeping it with him always, so that he remembers his matter. This practice is fitting for every person of deeds — for just as a merchant makes a ledger to account for his expenses, so a penitent should make a book to account for his days, whether he spent them properly or not, and by this fulfill "and my sin is always before me" (Psalms 51:5).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:32: Further, of this same category of discourse, one must be careful regarding excommunications and bans, and regarding the punishment for a ban, they elaborate in Pirkei D'Rabbi Eliezer (ch. 37): know the power of a ban — come and see from the tribes who were zealous over the licentiousness of the tribe of Benjamin. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them, "You were zealous over the licentiousness, but you were not zealous over Micah's idol" — and because they were not zealous over Micah's idol, the children of Benjamin killed among them a first, second, and third time, until they fell before the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord and sought repentance, and the Holy One, blessed be He, was reconciled with them, and they placed a ban that all Israel go to war against them, from the greatest to the smallest, as it is said, "for the great oath was that..." (Judges 21:5) — was it a literal oath that all Israel swore? Rather, this teaches you that the ban is [equivalent to] the oath, and the men of Yavesh-Gilead were not with them in the assembly and became liable to death, as it is said, "whoever came not up to the Lord at Mizpah shall surely be put to death" (Judges 21:5) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:33: Further there, in Pirkei D'Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Akiva says: the ban is the oath and the oath is the ban, and whoever breaks the oath is as though he broke the ban, and whoever breaks the ban breaks the oath; and whoever knows a matter and does not tell it, the ban comes upon him and destroys him and his timber and his stones, as it is said, "and I will send it forth, says the Lord, and it shall come into the house of the thief, and into the house of him who swears falsely by My Name, and it shall remain in the midst of his house and consume it, both timber and stones thereof" (Zechariah 5:4). Know the power of the ban — come and see from Joshua son of Nun, who placed a ban on Jericho — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:34: Further, one must be careful not to say, "I will be under a ban if I do not do such-and-such," for even if he fulfills the condition, it still requires formal annulment — and so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explain in tractate Makkot (11b): Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav, a ban, even conditional, requires annulment — from where do we learn this? From Judah, as it is written, "if I do not bring him to you and set him before you, then let me bear the blame forever" (Genesis 43:9), and it is written, "let Reuben live and not die... and this for Judah" (Deuteronomy 33:6-7) — all those forty years that Israel were in the desert, Judah's bones were rolling about in the coffin [unsettled] until Moses stood up for him and sought mercy, saying before Him, "Master of the universe, who caused Reuben to confess [his sin]? Judah did, by his own admission [regarding Tamar]" — immediately, "hear, Lord, the voice of Judah" — so far his words, as pertains to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:35: Further, one must be careful not to pronounce the Name according to its letters, as we learn in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah (17b): they brought Rabbi Chanina ben Teradion [before the Romans]; they said to him, "Why did you occupy yourself with Torah?" He said to them, "As the Lord my God commanded me." Immediately they decreed that he be burned, his wife executed, and his daughter placed in a brothel. He [was sentenced] to burning because he pronounced the Name according to its letters. But how could he have done this, when we have learned (Sanhedrin 10:1) that these have no share in the World to Come: one who says the Torah is not from Heaven, and one who denies the resurrection of the dead is derived from the Torah; Abba Shaul says, also one who pronounces the Name according to its letters [is excluded]? [The answer is:] he did so in order to learn it [privately], as it was taught, "you shall not learn to do" [i.e., to practice idolatrous or forbidden acts], but you may learn in order to understand and to teach [halachically] — so what then was the reason he was punished? Because he pronounced the Name publicly. And his wife [was sentenced] to execution because she did not protest against him — from here they said, whoever has the ability to protest and does not protest is punished for it — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:36: The Tosafot write (18a, s.v. "hogeh"): "pronouncing the Name" — one interpretation explains it as expounding it via the forty-two-letter Name and doing with it what he wishes; but most commentators explain that he was pronouncing the letters of the unique Name explicitly, like the letters of other words, and this is not proper to do, as we say in Pesachim (50a), "not as I am written am I called — I am written with Yod-Heh [i.e., YHVH] and called with Aleph-Dalet [i.e., Adonai]." It seems to Rabbeinu Yitzchak that one should not even utter the letters "Yod-Heh" as people commonly do, since "Yod-Heh" is itself the unique Name — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:37: "In order to learn" is permitted, as it was taught, and so on — and Rashi, of blessed memory, explains: nevertheless the Holy One, blessed be He, is exacting with the righteous to a hair's breadth, and even [an act done] for the purpose of learning still shows disregard for the honor of the Master; and the verse "you shall not learn to do" they applied to other matters, such as the planting of cucumbers in Sanhedrin (68a) and Rabban Gamliel's images of the moon (Rosh Hashanah 24a). And the Tosafot write that it seems that his text did not include the words "but what then was the reason he was punished — it was because he pronounced it publicly," and therefore he needed to give a different reason — so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:38: Further, one must be careful not to speak slander against Israel, and so it is said in Yalkut (Kings, remez 218): why is Israel likened to a nut? As it is said, "I went down into the garden of nuts" (Song of Songs 6:11) — just as this nut is smooth, and whoever is not skilled at climbing it immediately falls — one must guard oneself so as not to fall from it — so too whoever serves Israel must be careful not to take what is his from beneath their hand [i.e., not to profit at their expense through mistreatment]. Moses said, "hear now, you rebels" (Numbers 20:10), and it was said to him, "therefore you shall not bring this congregation into [the land]" (Numbers 20:12). Isaiah said, "and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips" (Isaiah 6:5) — immediately, "and in his hand a glowing coal" (Isaiah 6:6) — what is "retzafah" (the coal)? Rabbi Shimon bar Nachmani said [it hints at] "ratzatz peh" ("he crushed a mouth"), for he spoke slander against My children. Elijah said, "for the children of Israel have forsaken Your covenant" (I Kings 19:10), and what was he told? "And Elisha son of Shaphat shall you anoint as prophet in your place" (I Kings 19:16).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:39: Rabbi Yochanan derived this from this verse: "the burden of Damascus... it stands before Damascus, and proclaims the cities of Aroer" (Isaiah 17:1-2) — but is Aroer not only within the territory of Moab? Rather, there were three hundred sixty-five idol temples in Damascus, and they would worship each one on its own day; and they had one day where they worshiped them all — on that night the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, "Elijah, while you are still accusing My children, go your way to the wilderness of Damascus and accuse them there."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:40: Rabbi Abahu and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish were going up to Caesarea; Rabbi Abahu said to Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, "Why are we going up to a city of blasphemers and reviling?" Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish got down from his donkey, gathered up sand, and put it in his mouth. He said to him, "What is this?" He said to him, "The Holy One, blessed be He, does not desire whoever speaks slander against Israel," as it is written, "do not look upon me, that I am swarthy" (Song of Songs 1:6), and it is written, "do not slander a servant to his master" (Proverbs 30:10) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:41: There in Yalkut (Kings, remez 217), above, on the verse, "What are you doing here, Elijah?" (I Kings 19:9), it says: it was taught in the school of Elijah — he should have said before Him, "Master of the universe, behold, Your children, the children of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, have done Your will in Your world!" But he did not do so; rather, he said, "I have been very zealous..." and so on. The Holy One, blessed be He, began to speak words of comfort to him, saying, "When I came down to give the Torah, Israel did not descend with Me [in strict judgment], only the ministering angels who wished them well," as it is said, "go forth and stand upon the mountain..." and after the earthquake, fire — He waited for him three hours, and he still stood by his first words, saying, "I have been very zealous." The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, "And Elisha son of Shaphat shall you anoint as prophet in your place" — what you intend, you too may do [i.e., appoint your successor]. He said to Him, "You are forever zealous..." and so on — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:42: It is good for a person to train his tongue to teach merit on behalf of Israel, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, say in the Midrash Yelamdenu, regarding Gideon, who said, "and where are all His wonders?" (Judges 6:13), in these words: Rabbi Yehudah bar Shalom said, that night was Passover night, when he said, "and where are all His wonders?" — where are the wonders God did for our fathers on this night, when He struck all the firstborn of Egypt and brought Israel out joyfully? Since he taught merit on behalf of Israel, the Holy One, blessed be He, said, it is fitting that I reveal My glory to him, as it is said, "and the Lord turned to him and said, Go in this your might" (Judges 6:14). The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: you have the strength to teach merit on behalf of Israel; by your merit they shall be redeemed — this is [the meaning of] "and you shall save Israel" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:43: Further, we learn in Sanhedrin: Rabbi Acha said, we find that whoever teaches merit on behalf of Israel, the Holy One, blessed be He, exalts him in the world, as it is written, "and therefore the Lord will wait to be gracious to you, and therefore He will be exalted, to have mercy upon you" (Isaiah 30:18). From whom do you learn this? From Achimaatz son of Zadok, as it is said, "and Achimaatz son of Zadok said, Let me run and bring the king tidings... and he said, Is it well with the young man Absalom? And Achimaatz answered, I saw a great tumult... and the king said, Turn aside and stand here. So he turned aside and stood" (II Samuel 18:19, 29-30). Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said, if he had been a duke, he was made a prefect [i.e., promoted]; if a prefect, an istrelitos [general]. "And behold, the Cushite came, and the Cushite said, Tidings, my lord the king... and the king said to the Cushite, Is it well with the young man Absalom? And the Cushite answered, Let the enemies of my lord the king... be as that young man. And the king was much moved, and went up to the chamber over the gate, and wept" (II Samuel 18:31-32, 19:1). What is "the king was much moved"? Rabbi Yitzchak bar Chanina said, it hints at his executioners, whom he stabbed [in a fit of grief/rage]. Is this not an a fortiori argument? If Achimaatz, who spoke neither good nor bad about the king's son, merited all this honor, one who teaches merit on behalf of the children of the Omnipresent, all the more so! — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:44: And so in Vayikra Rabbah (Parashat 10:1), "Take Aaron," on the verse "you have loved righteousness and hated wickedness" (Psalms 45:8) — this verse is explained regarding Abraham, who sought merit for the people of Sodom, as explained there. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: you loved to declare My creatures righteous rather than to convict them; "therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of joy above your fellows" — what is "above your fellows"? He said to him, by your life, in ten generations from Noah to you, I did not speak with a single one of them, but with you I speak, as it is said, "after these things" [i.e., after Abraham's pleading for Sodom] (Genesis 15:1).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:45: Further it explains there this verse regarding Isaiah — that the Holy One, blessed be He, said, "Isaiah, My son, they are troublesome, they are stubborn; if you accept upon yourself to be shamed and struck by My children, you shall go on My mission, and if not, you shall not go on My mission." He said to Him, "On this condition [I accept] — 'I gave my back to the smiters and my cheeks to those who plucked out the hair' (Isaiah 50:6) — but I am not worthy to go on a mission to Your children." The Holy One, blessed be He, said, "Isaiah, you loved righteousness — you loved to declare My children righteous — 'and hated wickedness' — you hated to convict them — 'therefore God, your God, has anointed you' — what is 'above your fellows'?" He said to him: by your life, all the prophets received prophecy, prophet from prophet, [as it is written] "and He drew from the spirit that was upon him..." (Numbers 11:25), and "and they said, The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha" (II Kings 2:15) — but you, from the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He, directly: "the spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me..." (Isaiah 61:1). By your life, all the prophets [gave] simple prophecies, but you [give] doubled comforts: "awake, awake" (Isaiah 51:9), "arouse yourself, arouse yourself" (Isaiah 51:17), "I will greatly rejoice" (Isaiah 61:10), "I, even I, am He who comforts you" (Isaiah 51:12), "comfort, comfort" (Isaiah 40:1) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:46: Further, one must be careful not to converse idly in the synagogue, and so Rabbeinu Yaakov writes (Orach Chaim, siman 151): in synagogues and study halls one does not practice levity, such as laughter, jest, and idle talk. And in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah 131b), in these words: whoever converses in the synagogue, woe to him for showing separation, woe to him for diminishing faith, woe to him who has no portion in the God of Israel — for he shows that there is no God, that He is not found there, and he has no portion in Him and does not fear Him, and treats the supernal rectification above with contempt — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:47: Although from the wording it might appear that all these severities are stated only regarding the time of prayer, as it says just before this, that at the time Israel arrange in the synagogue the order of songs and praises and the order of prayer, then three camps of the supernal angels gather — nevertheless, since the synagogue is a holy place, the seat of the Shechinah, and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, forbade thinking about business calculations there at all times unless they are calculations for a mitzvah (Tur, ibid., see Megillah 28b), certainly one should not converse in idle worldly talk, or forbidden idle talk, even outside the synagogue, as it is written, "and you shall speak of them" (Deuteronomy 6:7) — and not of idle matters; from here, whoever converses in mundane speech or idle talk transgresses a positive commandment (see Yoma 19b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:48: The general principle that emerges is that wherever there is holiness, one must conduct oneself with awe, as it is written, "how awesome is this place! This is nothing else but the house of God" (Genesis 28:17). And in the commandments of Rashbi, peace be upon him (Zohar Parashat Beshalach 59b), it says that the synagogue below corresponds to the synagogue above; and when a person imagines this matter in his mind, he will fear and tremble and pray with intention — for the supernal synagogue is called "a fire of brightness" (esh nogah), and the souls of the righteous enter it only to pray, not to converse in idle words, and correspondingly the synagogue below is called "a fire of brightness," as is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Ki Tetze 282a), and therefore they call the synagogue "a fire of brightness."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:49: Rabbi Eliezer of Worms writes in Sefer HaRokeach (Hilchot Teshuvah): one who speaks in the synagogue while his companions praise and sing, I apply to him, "among all my evil neighbors" (Jeremiah 12:14), for "the ways of the Lord are right, and the righteous shall walk in them, but transgressors shall stumble in them" (Hosea 14:10); and one who does not join with his companions and disdains praising his Maker encroaches on the Creator's boundary — "and I shall be to them as a small sanctuary" (Ezekiel 11:16) — these synagogues, in which one does not practice levity, as we say in chapter 3 of Megillah (28b-29a). "God stands in the congregation of God" (Psalms 82:1) — and one who speaks acts as though he turns his back on Him; He will say, "why have I come, and there was no man? I called, and there was no one to answer" (Isaiah 50:2), "I have stretched out My hand, and no one paid attention" (Proverbs 1:24); "why should the Lord be angry at your voice, and cry out against you, 'who requires this of you, to trample My courts'" (cf. Isaiah 1:12)? Rather, bow down to Him and stand before Him in awe, with lowered head, in humility, with the innermost sight of your heart entreat Him, and sing before Him joyfully, and come before Him with joyful song — then He shall be near you and found for you, and you shall unify the Name of Heaven with the intention of your heart, and pray with the intention of your heart. And when you say "Blessed are You," if you think of idle matters, it is as though you mocked Him, for you did not place His fear upon your face; rather, think that He stands facing you — "I have set the Lord always before me" (Psalms 16:8) — and place His fear upon your face and His love within you, and direct your whole heart, and be modest before Him, and confess your sins and seek Him, and He is found for you, and bless Him — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:50: If this is not possible for everyone, at least Torah scholars who fear sin should take this matter to heart, and not begin speaking to one another in the synagogue about their affairs even outside the time of prayer, so as to conduct themselves with awe in the synagogue; and if someone who has not adopted this practice speaks to them, they should answer him briefly.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:51: This was likewise the practice of my teacher, peace be upon him: not to speak within the sukkah during the festival of Sukkot except in words of Torah, for the holiness of the commandment of the sukkah is great — the proof being that the wood of the sukkah has holiness attached to it and is forbidden [for other use] all seven days, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, say (Sukkah 9a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:52: And so we find that Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains (Zohar Parashat Emor, end of 103) that the Patriarchs come into the sukkah, and he says that Rav Hamnuna Sabba, when he would enter the sukkah, would rejoice and stand at the entrance of the sukkah from within, and say, "Let us invite the guests"; he would arrange the table and stand on his feet and bless, saying, "In sukkot you shall dwell — sit, supernal guests, sit, sit, guests of faith, sit"; he would raise his hands and rejoice and say, "Fortunate is our portion, fortunate is the portion of Israel," as it is written, "for the Lord's portion is His people" (Deuteronomy 32:9) — and he would sit down — so far his words. Above this, on the preceding page, he calls the sukkah "the shade of faith," and says that whoever sits beneath the shade of faith inherits freedom for himself and his children forever, and is blessed with a supernal blessing, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:53: This shows that a person within the sukkah is surrounded by an atmosphere of holiness, and there are so many holinesses within it, as explained; therefore it is fitting to distance oneself from idle talk and jest, but rather to fulfill "and rejoice with trembling" (Psalms 2:11) — for the mystery hinted at in the sukkah is joy and trembling, from which judgments are aroused (Zohar Parashat Acharei Mot 65a), and the days of Sukkot are days of judgment — the proof being that on Hoshana Rabbah night the judgment is sealed. These days must be spent in repentance and trembling, for these days were given so that a person might extend the time to repent, and the notes of decrees are not handed over to the messengers [for execution] until the eighth night of the festival of Atzeret, as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayechi 220a), in these words: come and see, when judgment is aroused in the world, the Holy One, blessed be He, sits on the throne of judgment, a person needs to arouse repentance through the judgment, to return from liability — for on that day [Rosh Hashanah] the notes are written and all are found in a state of anger, already written; whichever person returns before his Master, the notes concerning him are torn up. Afterward the Holy One, blessed be He, is ready before a person on the Day of Atonement, the day of repentance; if he returns from his sins, he returns [is spared], and if not, the King commands the notes to be sealed — woe, for repentance must be removed from him [i.e., its power to help is lessened]. If he merits complete repentance as is fitting, they hang [suspended] until that final day of Atzeret, which is the eighth day; and if he performs complete repentance before his Master, they are torn up; but if he does not merit it, those notes go out from the King's house and are handed into [the messengers'] hands, and judgment is carried out, and the notes do not return again to the King's house — then the images [decrees] are transmitted [for execution] — so far his words, as pertains to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:54: Further, one must be careful not to converse in mundane talk on Shabbat, and so it is explained in Midrash Tanchuma (beginning of Parashat Bereshit), on the verse, "and honor it, not doing your own ways, nor finding your own pleasure, nor speaking [idle] words" (Isaiah 58:13), in these words: "nor speaking words" — as with the mother of Rashbi, who, when she was speaking on Shabbat, he said to her, "It is the day of Shabbat, and one should keep silent." Rabbi Yochanan said, out of necessity they permitted greeting people on Shabbat — so far his words. And so the Tosafot quote this Midrash (s.v. "shelo yehei") in the chapter Elu Kesharim (Shabbat 113b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:55: Further, they say in the Midrash (see Pesikta Rabbati 23): just as He [ceased/rested] from speech [in a sense], so should you rest from speech [idle talk], for "by the word of the Lord the heavens were made" (Psalms 33:6), and His labor was speech; and what is said of Him, "and He rested on the seventh day" (Genesis 2:2), is a resting from speech — likewise a person should do the same.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:56: In the Zohar (Parashat Vayakhel 205b), in these words: when Israel enter the synagogue, it is forbidden to occupy themselves even with a need of the synagogue except with words of praise, prayer, and Torah, as is fitting for them; and whoever occupies himself with other matters and worldly matters is a person who desecrates the Sabbath, and has no portion among the people of Israel. Two angels are appointed over this on the day of Shabbat, and they place their hands upon his head and say, "Woe to so-and-so, who has no portion in the Holy One, blessed be He!" Therefore one should occupy oneself with prayer and with songs and praises of one's Master and occupy oneself with Torah — this day is the day of souls, when that bundle of souls is crowned with the praises of their Master; therefore they praise with praises of the soul, and this is [the verse] "the soul of every living thing shall bless Your Name, O Lord our God, and the spirit of all flesh" [from the liturgy] — and there is no praise except from the side of neshamah and ruach, and this day stands in ruach and neshamah, it is not of the body — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:57: For this reason we understand why our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Yerushalmi Shabbat 15:3), forbade asking for one's personal needs on Shabbat, so that on Shabbat one prays only seven blessings [in the Amidah, instead of the usual weekday nineteen] — because this day is the day of the neshamah and not the day of the body, and therefore one does not ask for the body's needs. From here the discerning reader can deduce that he should be stringent with himself regarding mundane talk — for if asking for the needs of one's own body is forbidden, mundane talk is all the more so.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:58: Further, one must be careful not to speak while the prayer leader repeats the Amidah, even words of Torah, but should intend to answer "Amen" to each and every blessing, with his ears attentive to what the prayer leader utters, and his eyes downward and his heart above, just as in his own silent prayer (Yevamot 105b). The reason is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas 229a), that these are two unifications, and in the repetition of the Amidah it is a more excellent unification than the previous one — for he answers "Amen" to every blessing, and "Amen" numerically equals the two Names YAKDONKY [combined], which does not happen when a person prays silently, for then he mentions the Lord only by His appellation Adonai, and even though his intention is toward YHVH, nevertheless the two Names are not interlinked as one; but with "Amen" it is a hint of the two Names being unified as one — it follows that this is a more excellent unification.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:59: These are the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, there, in brief: greater is one who answers "Amen" than the one who recites the blessing — for [it corresponds to] Adonai [and] YHVH in prayer, and their faces and their wings, corresponding to the Name YHVH in the faces, corresponding to the Name Adonai in the wings — "one cherub at one end, and one cherub at the other end" (Exodus 37:8); but when the prayer leader repeats the prayer and he answers "Amen," he is in the second joining — with "Amen" the two Names are joined in the second joining; at first they are like the loops corresponding one to another in the boards, which are the joints of the fingers, but with "Amen," "the Tabernacle shall be one" (Exodus 26:6), in which curtain is joined to curtain (Exodus 26:3) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:60: This makes explicit that the prayer leader's repetition of the prayer is a more excellent unification than the previous one, when he prayed silently — for the cherubim are "one cherub at one end," and so on; and if a person speaks during the prayer leader's repetition, he separates the unification, for there should be no other speech there except "Amen," which indicates the unification.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:61: It is likewise proven from here that when there is a repetition of the eighteen blessings by the prayer leader, one should not vary and say part of the prayer aloud to recite the Kedushah, and part silently — for such a prayer has no place either silently or aloud, and nothing like this is found either in the Gemara or in the Zohar.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:62: This is likewise proven in Parashat Vayelech (Zohar Parashat Vayelech 285b), that one must have an attentive ear to answer "Amen" to every blessing — for it says, on the verse "He who keeps faith (shomer emunim)" (Isaiah 26:2): meaning, he guards that blessing that the one reciting it says, and waits to answer "Amen" as needed; his soul ascends and proclaims before Him, "Open the gates..." and so on. And it further says: we have learned, whoever hears from the one reciting a blessing and does not intend an "Amen" for it, concerning him it is said, "and those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed" (I Samuel 2:30), as it is said, "to you, O priests, who despise My name" (Malachi 1:6); and at the time he is needed [to answer], what is his punishment? Just as he did not open the blessings above [i.e., did not participate], so they do not open for him. And not only that, but when he departs from this world, they proclaim before him and say, "Shut the gates before so-and-so, let him not enter, and do not receive him!" Woe to him, woe to his soul — so far his words. They further elaborate there on his punishment.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:63: The wise person's eyes are in his head, and he should weigh whether occupation with Torah during the time of prayer is greater or answering "Amen" — and certainly they are not of the same category for the time of prayer, for "a word in its proper time, how good it is" (Proverbs 15:23). It seems to me that Rabbeinu Yonah intended this when he said, "fortunate is he whose toil is in Torah and who gives satisfaction to his Creator" (Berachot 17a) — that his toil in Torah should be a satisfaction to his Creator — excluding when he occupies himself with Torah at a time when the Holy One, blessed be He, does not desire his Torah study, in the aforementioned aspects — then certainly there is no satisfaction to the Holy One, blessed be He, in his Torah study, and it would be better for him not to occupy himself with Torah [at that moment].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:64: Just as one must be careful during any repetition by the prayer leader not to speak, so one must be careful on Sabbath night when the prayer leader repeats "Vaychulu" ("And they were finished") — for it is written in Sefer Chasidim that a certain pious man saw another pious man like himself, after he died, with his face yellowish; he said to him, "Why is your face yellowish?" He said to him, "Because I used to speak during 'Vaychulu' when the congregation recites it, and during the blessing 'Magen Avot,' and during 'Yitgadal' [the Kaddish]" — so far. This is how Rabbeinu Yaakov quotes this wording (Tur Orach Chaim, siman 268).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:65: Further, one must be careful not to speak during the reading of the Torah scroll, and they are stringent about this in the Zohar — see there (Parashat Pinchas 229a), in these words, in Parashat Vayakhel (206a): when the Torah scroll is raised there, then all the people must arrange themselves with awe, with fear, with trembling and quaking, all below, and direct their hearts as though they now stood at Mount Sinai to receive the Torah, listening and inclining their ears; and no one, whether of the congregation or otherwise, has permission to open his mouth in Torah, all the more so in another matter, but all should be in awe as though they had no mouth — and this has already been established, as it is written, "and when he opened it, all the people stood..." (Nehemiah 8:5), "and the ears of all the people were attentive to the book of the Torah" (Nehemiah 8:3) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:66: Further, one must be careful, when occupied with Torah or prayer, to utter the words of Torah and prayer in their proper form, not hastily and swallowed — and they say in the Zohar (Parashat Pinchas 227a) that just as the body benefits from bread after the wheat has been ground and the fine flour separated from the bran and all the husks, so one must grind the words of Torah with one's teeth until the neshamah benefits from them. In these words: the third, fine kelipah, corresponds to the bran of the wheat, for it clings to the wheat and cannot be separated from it until they are ground in millstones, which correspond to the grinding [teeth] of the mouth, for a person must grind the words of Torah with them until they become like fine flour, and with a sieve, which is the lip, the refuse, the bran of the Torah, is separated out, until halachah is found to be pure fine flour. At that time the heart and brain and all the limbs of the body, into which the neshamah spreads, take it — in the manner that the body is sustained by worldly words, for "one corresponding to the other has God made" (Ecclesiastes 7:14) — the bread of the body and the bread of Torah — this is what is written, "come, eat of my bread" (Proverbs 9:5) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:67: Further there (Zohar Parashat Pinchas 236a): from here, whoever utters words of Torah must grind them with his teeth and produce complete words, and these words are called "complete"; but others, who are foolish and swallow words in a gulp and do not grind them with their millstones and their teeth — what is written of them? "The meat was yet between their teeth..." and "the anger of the Lord was kindled against the people" (Numbers 11:33) — these are of the stock of one who said, "let me gulp down (halei'teini)" (Genesis 25:30) — so far his words. And this is likewise brought in this wording in the same passage (Zohar Parashat Pinchas 246a) — see there.
